conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because you’ve been feeling unwell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you for coming. It started this weekend—this strange 'wavy' feeling, like my whole body was off. Not dizzy, not lightheaded, just… unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it reminded you of how you felt before getting septic in the past. That’s a very valid concern, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I’ve been through that before, and I don’t want to miss the early signs again. But my G-tube and femoral line look fine—no redness, no discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, that’s reassuring. The triage temperature of 100.4 was repeated and came back normal at 98.5, so no fever. Your labs, EKG, and urine were all unremarkable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’ve also had these episodes—head shaking, like nodding uncontrollably. I can’t stop it. It’s scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve actually seen one of those episodes earlier. You were fully awake, answering questions, and your vitals stayed stable. That’s very important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was aware the whole time. It’s not like my old pseudoseizures—they were different. But I’m worried… my brother had glioblastoma. Could this be something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand that fear. But your recent head CT was normal, and there’s no sign of a tumor. These episodes don’t look like seizures or anything malignant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what could it be? It feels so real when it happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be a benign movement issue—something like a tremor or myoclonus. We’ll set up a follow-up with your neurologist in two weeks to go over it in detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thank you. I just want to make sure it’s not something dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve also checked your abdomen. You have some tenderness, but your G-tube is working fine, and there’s no sign of infection or acute obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about this small lump in my lower right belly. It’s been there a while, but I keep thinking it could be something bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We felt that. It’s about 2 cm, soft, and not tender. Given your history of multiple surgeries, it’s most likely scar tissue. You already have an outpatient biopsy scheduled—good plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. And my femoral line? I’ve had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Site looks clean, no redness or swelling. You’re on Lovenox 40 mg daily, which you tolerate well. We’ll keep that going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I bruise easily on higher doses, so this is what my doctor and I agreed on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. We’ve continued all your home meds—topiramate for migraines, levothyroxine, gabapentin, and the rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a few migraines lately too. Usually with visual aura. I’ve been using sumatriptan as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that available. Your current symptoms don’t seem to be migraine-related, but we’re managing them as part of your overall care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your blood cultures—both came back with no growth. That’s excellent news—no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. I was really worried about sepsis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We also did orthostatics—your blood pressure stayed stable when you stood up. So not related to low blood pressure or dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the head shaking? Did you see it again last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse and I both saw it. You were alert, talking, and vitals were normal. Still no signs of seizure activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad you saw it. I was afraid no one would believe me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. It’s real, and we’re taking it seriously. But based on what we’ve seen, it’s not dangerous. Your neurologist will help figure out what’s causing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ve been stable, labs are normal, and we’ve ruled out serious causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel better, but I’m still nervous about the head shaking at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But remember, you’re safe. The episodes don’t affect your breathing or consciousness. And your neuro follow-up is already set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my G-tube and line? Should I watch for anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on the sites—redness, swelling, or drainage would be a reason to call. But they looked perfect today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the abdominal distention? The X-ray showed gassy bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s some distention, but no obstruction or free air. Likely related to your chronic motility issues. We’ll keep managing it as before—your TPN and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Physical therapy saw you this morning and says you’re safe to ambulate independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ll follow up with my neurologist and get that nodule checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you have any new symptoms—fever, severe pain, or changes in the shaking—don’t hesitate to call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and not dismissing my concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You know your body best. We’re here to support you, not ignore you. Take care, and I’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
